questions.q: According to NIST's AI Risk Management Framework, how are security and fairness characteristics of a trustworthy AI system presented?
options: As two entirely separate frameworks with no connection to each other
Fairness is only mentioned in a footnote, with no formal status in the framework
As part of one unified list of interdependent trustworthy AI characteristics, not separate tracks
Security is covered by NIST, but fairness is explicitly excluded from the AI RMF entirely
questions.explain: NIST names one set of characteristics — valid/reliable, safe, secure/resilient, accountable/transparent, explainable/interpretable, privacy-enhanced, and fair with harmful bias managed — presented together as interdependent, not as separate frameworks.

questions.q: Why does missing audit logging cause problems for both security and fairness reviews?
options: It doesn't — audit logging is only relevant to security investigations, never to fairness
Because audit logging is required only for fairness audits and has no security purpose
Because logging only affects system performance, not any kind of investigation
Because without it, you can't investigate either a suspected prompt-injection incident or a complaint that the system behaved differently for different users
questions.explain: The same missing control — audit logging — blocks investigation of a security incident and a fairness complaint alike, because both investigations depend on being able to trace what the system actually did.

questions.q: What does this lesson identify as the practical similarity between red-teaming and a bias audit?
options: They use the same methodology — systematically probing a system with input and checking the output against an expectation — pointed at a different risk category
A bias audit requires no testing at all, unlike red-teaming
Red-teaming and bias audits are unrelated activities performed by unrelated disciplines with nothing in common
Bias audits can only be performed on models that have never been red-teamed
questions.explain: Both are the same kind of systematic adversarial-input testing: red-teaming checks output against security policy, a bias audit checks output for unwarranted differences across groups.

questions.q: What does the lesson mean by calling a biased model and an insecure model 'symptoms of the same underlying problem'?
options: That bias and insecurity are always caused by exactly the same line of code
That inadequate governance — missing logging, missing documentation, missing testing — can produce both failures from the same root gap, rather than two unrelated problems
That a model cannot be insecure unless it is also biased
That fairness problems always resolve automatically once a system is made secure
questions.explain: The lesson's examples (missing logging, missing documentation, missing the equivalent of red-teaming for bias) show the same governance gap producing both kinds of failure, not an automatic link between the two.

questions.q: What does this lesson say should result from treating responsible AI and AI security as one connected governance discipline?
options: The same board, threat-modeling inputs, and category of adversarial testing cover both, instead of running two disconnected review tracks
Fairness review becomes entirely unnecessary once security review is complete
Security review becomes entirely unnecessary once fairness review is complete
Two separate boards should be created, each with no visibility into the other's findings
questions.explain: The lesson's point is unification: one governance program, reviewed by one board, using the same threat-modeling and adversarial-testing inputs for both security and fairness — not two disconnected tracks.
